claims.text: Melt spinning at cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s can produce amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Slower cooling of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 produces a complex crystalline microstructure containing multiple phases.
The phases formed during slower cooling are several primary non-eutectic phases.
Conventional reheating of melt-spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 produces extensive primary crystallization through a complex, multistep sequence.
Cooling at or above 10^5 K/s ensures full amorphization of this alloy.
Approximately 960 K is the eutectic crystallization temperature observed for this alloy under slower cooling.
A millisecond-to-one-second flash-annealing pulse below approximately 960 K can access a structural-relaxation regime without causing crystallization.
Post-solidification flash annealing will reduce the density or activity of embryonic crystalline nuclei.
Flash annealing will enhance short-range atomic rearrangements and homogenize and relax the amorphous matrix.
The short flash pulse permits structural relaxation while leaving insufficient time for nucleation and growth of primary phases.
Flash annealing relieves internal stresses in the amorphous alloy.
Stress relief and structural relaxation minimize the driving force for crystallization and stabilize the disordered state.
Flash-annealed samples will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than conventionally reheated, non-flash-annealed samples.
Flash-annealed samples will have a lower crystalline phase fraction detectable by XRD and TEM.
Flash annealing will improve thermal stability and retention of the amorphous state.
Longer pulses or dwelling at nucleation-favorable temperatures could negate the proposed benefit by permitting crystallization.
